title: The energy transition
subtitle: Toward carbon neutrality
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: The world is trying to replace fossil fuels with cleaner sources. A shift as necessary as it is difficult.

hero.hook: Solar has become the cheapest energy in history. Storing it is the hard part.

blocks.text: For a long time humanity changed its energy source by choice, for efficiency: from wood to coal, then from coal to oil. Today's **energy transition** is different: for the first time it is imposed by a question of survival, climate change.
This course explores how the world is trying to replace fossil fuels with cleaner sources, and why that shift is as hard as it is necessary.

The framework that now guides every energy policy is the **[[Paris Agreement (2015)]]**. The treaty commits the countries of the world to limiting global warming, with one precise goal: to stay below 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels if at all possible. Every extra tenth of a degree makes extreme weather worse.

blocks.caption: Solar panels and wind turbines, symbols of the world's shift to low-carbon energy sources

blocks.text: To meet that goal, states aim at **[[carbon neutrality]]**: a balance between the greenhouse gases released by human activity and the amount absorbed by forests, soils, oceans or capture technology. It means global emissions must stop rising before 2025, then fall sharply in the years after.

The cost of solar energy fell 90% between 2010 and 2020, faster than almost any other technology in economic history. By 2023, solar had become the cheapest source of electricity ever produced in many parts of the world.

The main engine of the transition is economic. **Photovoltaic solar**, once reserved for satellites, has seen its price divided by ten in fifteen years, thanks to technical progress and economies of scale. **Wind power**, especially offshore where the winds are stronger and steadier, has also reached real industrial maturity. In 2023, nearly 90% of the new electricity capacity installed worldwide already came from renewables.

One large challenge remains: solar and wind suffer from **intermittency**, meaning they do not produce electricity continuously. Hence the importance of large batteries, whose price has followed the same spectacular fall as solar, making electric cars more and more competitive.

China now makes more than 80% of the world's solar panels and more than 70% of the lithium-ion batteries for electric vehicles. The energy transition of the West therefore depends heavily on a Chinese manufacturing chain.

sections.title: The new obstacles: storage and rare metals

blocks.text: Despite the enthusiasm, the transition runs into real limits. Unlike gas or coal, which can be burned at will, renewables need more flexible electricity grids, with storage or backup sources such as hydrogen and nuclear power.

Another obstacle is the move from a dependence on oil to a dependence on **[[rare earth elements]]** and other metals, such as lithium and cobalt, needed to build batteries and wind turbines. China controls an enormous share of the world refining of these materials, which creates new weak points for Europe and the United States.

Finally, the transition meets social resistance: fossil fuel industries still employ millions of people, and transforming those jobs without destroying them is an essential condition for the transition to be accepted by everyone.

The energy future probably rests not on a single solution but on a blend of several. **[[Green hydrogen]]** looks like a key piece for decarbonizing the hardest sectors, such as steelmaking and aviation, where electricity alone is not enough.
The transition also calls for **restraint**: using less and using it better, by insulating buildings or cutting industrial waste, is often the most effective and the cheapest lever.

Some experimental batteries run on gravity: they use the day's surplus of solar power to hoist heavy concrete blocks into the air, then let them come back down in the evening, driving a turbine that makes electricity.

The cost of solar fell 90% in fifteen years, making it the cheapest source of electricity in history. But storing energy and securing supplies of rare metals remain the great challenges of the energy transition.
